source_text: Cum anima, inquit, patris mea sit et anima filii mea sit, quo testimonio ut multis aliis docetur animam nihil debere seminibus, quam Deus iuri suo vindicat, iniquissimum, inquit, et stolidum est, ut mea res, mea imago alienis gravetur operibus.
pass_a_gloss: Since the soul, he says, of the father is mine and the soul of the son is mine—by which testimony as by many others it is taught that the soul owes nothing to seeds, which God vindicates to his own right—it is most unjust, he says, and stupid, that my thing, my image, be burdened by others' works.

lemmas.lexica: LS anima; Blaise human soul as image

pass_b_english: He says: Since the father’s soul is mine and the son’s soul is mine, it is utterly unjust and foolish for my possession, my image, to be burdened with another’s deeds. This testimony, like many others, teaches that the soul owes nothing to reproductive seed, since God claims it for his own authority (Genesis 1:26–27) (Ezekiel 18:4).

choices.why: Loaded word in Julian's Latin at this locus; English follows LS/Blaise range without copying NPNF.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: God calls the soul his image.
Repeats God’s ownership of the father’s and son’s souls.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
